A mutable *field* of an object is still outside the transaction (`VarCodeGen.MutableFieldVar:202-231`): decision 2 above, verified both ways by `probes/P10Field.fss` and under `walk`, and written out as a ledger row in `record.md`.

`atomic` used as an expression -- `atomic x := 1` rather than `atomic do x := 1 end` -- still has no visitor in `CodeGen` and reaches `defaultCase` (`map/spec-to-implementation.md:176`). Both new tests use the block form for that reason. `compiler_tests/Compiled170.fss`, which the inherited test comment cited as its model, is one of the programs that cannot compile for this reason and is in no `.test` file; the citation is gone.

Abrupt completion of an `atomic` block by a Fortress exception leaves the block's writes **visible**, which is the opposite of what the specification says, and this round measured it rather than speculating. `forAtomicBlock` catches only `TransactionAbortException` (the type at `CodeGen.java:1735`, registered as the sole handler at `:1738`), so an `FException` propagates out without `cleanupTransaction` ever running and the orphaned transaction stays current on the task; a later read of the variable therefore goes through `TXRead` and finds the transaction's own uncommitted write. `probes/skep

The compiled world cannot render an object or trait value that has no `asString` of its own: `FValue.toString` (`runtimeValues/FValue.java:25-27`) calls `asString()`, `trait Object`'s default `asString` is `jAsString(self)` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:338`), `jAsString` is bound to `stringOps.asString` (`:270`), and that helper returns `a.toString()` (`nativeHelpers/stringOps.java:38-40`, under the team's own "this can't be right! DRC"). The cycle is pre-existing and this round did not repair it; it removed the entry that R1 had opened into it. Reached from user code with no transacti

**Repairing the prelude and three corpus files rather than stopping.**  The alternative was

forced in any case: with `CompilerLibrary.fss:569` as written, `ZZ32_MIN`'s class

at all.  The decision is recorded here because it widens the rung past the two files the
brief named.

**Value-preserving rewrites in the corpus, not moves to `not_working_library_tests/`.**
Moving `Integer3` and `Integer4` was the alternative.  It was rejected because a faithful
rewrite exists and is exact, and because those two files are the only tests of the
`BOXPLUS`/`BOXMINUS`/`BOXDOT`/`DOTPLUS` wrapping and saturating operators at `ZZ32` and
`ZZ64` (`Integer3.fss:97-126`), which is coverage the corpus would not get back.

**`asNN32` repaired although nothing forced it.**  The alternative was to leave a vacuous
range check in place beside a repaired `asNN64`.  It was rejected because the check is
three lines from the comment that asks for this rung — "This is a cheap fix. Problem in
codeGen.forIntLiteral" (`FIntLiteral.java:79` before the repair) — and because leaving it
would keep a silent truncation (`probes/r2d`) in the one getter the rung was already
rewriting.  The report says plainly that this is a decision and that the brief's premise
about it, that `asNN32` "currently depends on the wrap" and would "begin throwing", is true
of `asNN64` and not of `asNN32`.

**Three branches kept, not collapsed to `simpleIntLiteralArith`'s two.**
`FIntLiteral.make(int)` and `make(long)` both store a `long`, so the int branch buys nothing
at run time and the two-branch form would have been a smaller edit.  It is kept because the
bytecode optimizer matches on it: `RemoveLiteralCoercions.removeIntLiterals`
(`compiler/asmbytecodeoptimizer/RemoveLiteralCoercions.java:33-53`) replaces
`FIntLiteral.make(I)` followed by `coerce_ZZ32` with `FZZ32.make(I)`, and collapsing the int
branch would switch that substitution off for every small literal.  The repair also makes

int branch is the `ZZ32`-representable range — true under `l <= 31`, false under `l <= 32`.

reached only from `ByteCodeOptimizer.main` (`ByteCodeOptimizer.java:130,146`), nothing in

**All fourteen sites of `Transaction.java`, not the nine that can crash.** Nine stringify a Fortress value or a table of them (`:162, :166, :185, :203, :227, :232, :249, :265, :274`) and are the entries into the cycle; `:232` renders both hash tables whole. **`BaseTask.java`'s eight remaining sites too.** None of them can crash -- I checked the one place where that could be true: `startTransaction`, `endTransaction` and `cleanupTransaction` (`BaseTask.java:180-212`) concatenate `" trans = " + transaction`, and `Transaction.toString` (`Transaction.java:61-63`) renders the transaction number and its parent, never the tables. range check is made to mean what it says.

### atomic.tex:36-44
An \KWD{atomic} expression consists of \KWD{atomic}
followed by a \emph{body expression}.  Evaluating an \KWD{atomic}
expression is simply evaluating the body expression.  All reads and
all writes which occur as part of this evaluation will appear to occur
simultaneously in a single atomic step with respect to \emph{any}
action performed by any thread which is dynamically outside.  This is
specified in detail in \chapref{memory-model}.  The value and type of an
\KWD{atomic} expression are the value and type of its body expression.


### atomic.tex:57-70
functional must not have both \KWD{atomic} and \KWD{io} modifiers.

When the body of an \KWD{atomic} expression completes abruptly, the
\KWD{atomic} expression completes abruptly in the same way.  If it
completes abruptly by exiting to an enclosing \KWD{label} expression,
writes within the block are retained and become visible to other
threads.  If it completes abruptly by throwing an uncaught exception,
all writes to objects allocated before the \KWD{atomic}
expression began evaluation are discarded.  Writes to newly
allocated objects are retained.  Any variable reverts to the value it
held before evaluation of the \KWD{atomic} expression began.  Thus, the
only values retained from the abruptly completed \KWD{atomic} expression
will be reachable from the exception object through a chain of newly
allocated objects.

### atomic.tex:75-83
expression but dynamically inside an enclosing \KWD{atomic}.

Implicit threads may be created dynamically within an \KWD{atomic}
expression.  These implicit threads will complete before the
\KWD{atomic} expression itself does so.  The implicit threads may
run in parallel, and will see one another's writes; they may
synchronize with one another using nested \KWD{atomic} expressions.

Note that \KWD{atomic} expressions may be evaluated in parallel with

### memory-model.tex:32-44
\section{Principles}

The Fortress memory model has been written with several important
guiding principles in mind.  Violations of these principles must be
taken as a flaw in the memory model specification rather than an
opportunity to be exploited by the programmer or implementor.  The most
important principle is this: violations of the Fortress memory model
must still respect the underlying data abstractions of the Fortress
programming language.  All data structures must be properly
initialized before they can be read by another thread, and a program
must not read values that were never written.  When a program fails,
it must fail gracefully by throwing an exception.


### memory-model.tex:67-77

  threads need not make the array elements shared; only elements
  actually accessed by more than one thread are considered to be

\seclabel{initialization}

To ensure that all objects and all variables are initialized before their
use, execution of program components
proceeds according to the procedure defined in this section.
This procedure assumes that the program's type hierarchy is already checked
to be acyclic.


If a component is a compound component,
all constituent components are initialized nondeterministically, but before
first use.
If a simple component has imports,
take the transitive closure of all imported \apisN.  Collect all
  declarations in this transitive closure, in any order, and prepend
  them to the component definition.
Finally, for a simple component without imports,
initialize all top-level variables and singleton object fields.

## 9. What it is expected to buy

Measured, and firm: against the honest baseline of one gate per rung, 8 × 582 s = 77.6 minutes, batches of four cost two gates, 19.4 minutes. **The saving is 58.2 minutes.** The 130.5-minute figure is what the last climb actually spent including redundancy the free fixes remove, and comparing against it would overstate this design's contribution.

Estimate, not measurement: with the gate lifted out, a rung worker's tool time is the 145 s cold seed plus a rebuild, its test and its subset; two run at a time; so eight rungs take four waves of workers and four of skeptics. Coarsely that is a climb of about two hours against 8h37m, and every term in it is an estimate built on measured parts.

Not estimated: what the probe now running removes from the gate itself.

## Where the fix belongs, answered before the edit

`map/spec-to-implementation.md:166` gives numerals their row: parser `Literal.rats:53`
`NumericLiteralExpr`, checker `Misc.scala:460-481`, interpreter
`Evaluator.forIntLiteralExpr:1506`, codegen `CodeGen.forIntLiteralExpr:3859`, prelude
`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:369` `trait IntLiteral`.

It is not in the parser or the AST: the node carries the value as a `BigInteger`
(`x.getIntVal()`), and the interpreter reads the same node and prints the true value
(`probes/r2a.walk.before`).

It is not in the folding phase, which is wired before `TYPECHECK` on the compile path only
(`compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java:57,142-143`) and computes in `BigInteger` on
`getIntVal()` (`compiler/desugarer/IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java:31,60-61`, arithmetic
from `:63`): it is exact, and measurably so — before the repair the folded expression
`4294967295 + 1` already printed `4294967296` while the same arithmetic through two
bindings printed `0` (`probes/r2e.compiled.before`).

It is not in the checker: every numeral gets the one flat type `Types.INT_LITERAL`
(`scala_src/typechecker/impls/Misc.scala:467-468`) and the compiler world's `IntLiteral`
trait has six abstract getters and no static parameter
(`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:370-376`), so nothing in the static
types carries the value a checker would have to range-check.  The specification's numeral
types do carry it (`literals.tex:83-86`), which is why on this path the diagnostic can only
be a run-time one; that gap is recorded below, not repaired.

It is not in the prelude's coercions: the five that read a numeral
(`CompilerBuiltin.fss:501` `ZZ`, `:562` `ZZ64`, `:620` `ZZ32`, `:684` `NN32`, `:747` `NN64`)
all run after the value has already been wrapped.

So the fix belongs at the code generator's own site, and in the runtime value it
constructs, `compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral`, whose two unsigned getters decoded the
wrap.

## Precedent search: the same decision, three times in this tree

The question "which representation carries a numeral's `BigInteger` value" is decided in
three places, and two of them are right.

`interpreter/evaluator/values/FIntLiteral.make(BigInteger)`
(`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/FIntLiteral.java:40-56`)
compares against `INT_MIN`/`INT_MAX` and `LONG_MIN`/`LONG_MAX` declared at `:21-27`, which
is exact for both signs.

`nativeHelpers/simpleIntLiteralArith.fromBigInteger`
(`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntLiteralArith.java:30-33`),
written by rung 7, uses `bitLength() < 64` for the long slot and the decimal string above
it, which is exact for both signs and numerically the same boundary as `<= 63`.

`CodeGen.forIntLiteralExpr` used `<= 32` and `<= 64`, which is the wrong one, and the
comment above it recorded that its author was unsure.

A fourth precedent is inside the runtime value itself: `FIntLiteral.asZZ64` (`:74-77`) tests
`largerVal == null` before narrowing, and `asRR64`/`asRR32` (`:101-110`) read `largerVal`
when it is present.  That is the shape `asNN64` now takes.

For the second half of the rung — how to write a bounded type's extreme value — the
precedent is `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:703-704`: `getter minimum(): ZZ64 =
-9223372036854775807 - 1` and `maximum(): ZZ64 = 9223372036854775807`, a numeral in range
and then one subtraction.  `library_tests/Integer3.fss:49-50` uses the same shape
(`maxValue: ZZ32 = 7FFFFFFF_16`, `minValue: ZZ32 = -maxValue - 1`) three lines below the
declaration this rung had to repair.

input.content:
<!-- Did the repair batch's re-architected briefs fix what the conformance review found, and where did its
     time go.  Written 2026-09-19 by a review worker at Pavol's request ("we had hopes that it would improve
     the failures that led to the need of repair ... whether we have achieved this goal with this
     re-architecture"), with the efficiency half asked for in the same breath.  Instruments and method are
     those of coordinator/iteration-cost.md and coordinator/next-climb/provenance.md, so the numbers compare.
     Read-only: no source was edited, no build or test was run.  One line per paragraph. -->

# The repair batch, reviewed

## The answer

**Yes on the brief's own terms, and the three numbers that show it are these.** The specification's prose chapters were opened in **56 of 955 tool calls (5.9%)** against **7 of 1,638 (0.4%)** in the eight-rung climb, and the api listings — the circular authority the review objected to — were cited **0 times** against 18. The territory map, opened by **none** of the last climb's 36 agents in the four parts the review named, was opened in **15 calls by 8 of this batch's 11 agents**. And **22 sentences** in the two `REPORT.md` files and `JUDGE.md` name a decision as a decision with its alternative, against **0** in the nine reports of the last climb. Both owed repairs landed, gated green, with four new gated tests; the specification citations in the landed record were opened at the lines cited in **18 of 20** cases, against three wrong of eight last time.

**The cost was wall-clock, not rigor.** The batch took **235.4 minutes** for two rungs where the old serial loop would have taken about **150** for the same two (`iteration-cost.md` §A: rung 3 at 66.3 min and rung 7 at 52.0 min, the two `.java` rungs, plus the repair-and-verify2 pair at 32.0 min for its one refusal). It spent that on **2.3× the tool calls per rung** — 478 against 205 — and on **68 differential probe programs** the last climb had no counterpart for. The gate fell from **25.2% of the clock to 5.2%**, and the four redundancies the last review priced at 41.0 minutes are all gone: zero `ant` runs piped through `tail`, one gate for two rungs, one repeated command in 955.

**What did not take.** The design-intent corpus — `Papers/`, `research/`, the spec's `\note{}` passages, `map/design-intent-sources.md` — is still almost unread: **0 calls** to the first three, one grep of the fourth. That is the part of the review's diagnosis the re-architecture did not move, and it is the part `map/design-intent-sources.md:100` says holds the rationale.

Every number below is regenerated by one command:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/repair-batch-review/parse.py \
      --root /root/.claude/projects/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/subagents/workflows \
      --out  explorations/coordinator/repair-batch-review

The per-agent table it writes is `repair-batch-review/agents.csv`. Sources: the three workflow transcript directories under that root — `wf_aabc0cb2-d31` (the relaunch that landed, 11 agents), `wf_9777a563-c5e` (the launch of 22:57 cut at 23:22 by the platform restart, 2 agents), `wf_9b6732fc-64c` (confirmed from its `journal.jsonl` and metas to be the four-trivial-agent concurrency probe: `probe:0` and `probe:1` start together at 19:14:02 and 19:14:05, `probe:2` only at 19:14:26 after `probe:0` ends at 19:14:25, so the harness's cap of two is measured, not assumed) — plus the landed commits `49ee5e91..63db7a691` and the two rung directories.

# Part 1 — provenance and quality

## 1. What the batch opened, beside the last climb

| what | last climb, 36 agents, 1,638 calls | this batch, 11 agents, 955 calls |
|---|---|---|
| any path under `Specification/` | 32 (2.0%) | 58 (6.1%) |
| — prose chapters (`basic/`, `basic-lib/`, …) | 7, all in one repair after review | **56, in 9 of 11 agents** |
| — `library/apis/` listings | 18 | **0** |
| — repo-wide greps under `Specification/` | 7 | 2 |
| `map/spec-to-implementation.md` | 0 | 4 |
| `map/modules-and-phases.md` | 0 | 7 |
| `map/test-coverage.md` | 0 | 2 |
| `map/dormant-code.md` | 7 planners | 3 |
| `map/design-intent-sources.md` | 0 | 1 (one grep, by `rung:R2`) |
| interpreter library (`FortressLibrary.*`, `FortressBuiltin.*`) | 77 | 17 |
| `Papers/`, `research/`, `\note{}` passages | 0 | 0 |

The ratio is what moved. The last climb consulted the interpreter's library about eleven times for every prose citation (77 against 7); this batch consulted the prose about three times for every interpreter read (56 against 17). Rule 3 of the prefix held absolutely: not one call in either launch opened `Specification/library/`.

Per agent, prose-chapter calls: `rung:R1` 18, `rung:R2` 9, `skeptic:R2` 8, `repair:R1` 6, `skeptic:R1` 4, `judge:R1` 3, `skeptic2:R1` 3, `gather` 3, `review` 2, `gate` 0, `commit` 0. Three of the last climb's eight rungs opened no `Specification/` file at all; here every agent that judged or wrote code opened one.

## 2. The four rules, per rung worker, from the transcript order

| rule | R1 (relaunch) | R2 (relaunch) | R1 repair round |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. "where does this fix belong", before the first source edit | spec prose 23:29:56, map 23:35:34, first source edit **00:02:02** — 32 min of orientation first | spec prose 23:30:30, `dormant-code` 23:33:17, first source edit **23:42:37**; `spec-to-implementation.md` at 23:43:21, **44 s after** | spec prose 01:39:59, `modules-and-phases` 01:47:55, guards edited 01:41:09 — spec first, map after |
| 2. precedent search by citation, before the edit | three `VarCodeGen` shapes cited at line (`REPORT.md:42-46`); **missed rung 0's guard**, which is the refusal | four cited: interpreter `FIntLiteral:40-56`, `simpleIntLiteralArith:30-33`, `CodeGen`'s wrong one, `FIntLiteral.asZZ64:74-77`; plus `FortressLibrary.fss:703-704` for the prelude spelling | rung 0's `BaseTask.java:248`, cited from `rung0/REPORT.md:11`, `FACTS.md:14`, row 302 |
| 3. api listings cited as the standard | never; 0 calls to `Specification/library/` in the whole batch | never | never |
| 4. every cited `file:line` opened before being written | yes (see §6) | yes, except the two CHOOSE lines its skeptic wrote | yes |

R2's ordering deserves the caveat. The `.java` bounds edit was inherited from the cut launch, whose own worker read `literals.tex` at 22:59:52 and `map/spec-to-implementation.md` at 23:00:04, thirteen minutes before it first edited source at 23:13:05; the relaunched worker re-read the map row 44 seconds after its second-half prelude edit. So `REPORT.md:67`'s heading "answered before the edit" is true of the rung read across both launches and not of the relaunched agent alone.

## 3. The skeptics

Both skeptics wrote and ran their own differentials, which is the requirement four of the last climb's highest-value findings came from. **R1's skeptic wrote 25 probe programs in its first judgement and 7 more in its second; R2's wrote 10.** Against 26 worker probes (17 + 9), the batch's 68 probe programs are its main instrument.

R1's first skeptic **refused**, on one ground, with nine findings; its second judgement approved with three required corrections and seven fresh probes. R2's skeptic approved with four required corrections and three recommendations. Classified:

| class | count | which |
|---|---|---|
| regression | 1 | R1 finding 1: `atomic` on an object- or trait-typed top-level variable became a `StackOverflowError` |
| specification violation | 2 | `atomic` as a `do … also` arm's trailing expression does not verify (row 322); `IntLiteral` comparison at `ZZ64` throws where the spec requires `false` (row 328) |
| specification settles it against the interpreter | 3 | `walk` rejects a forward singleton-field initializer (row 323); `CHOOSE` for k > m ≥ 0; `walk` refuses `d: ZZ32 = -2147483648` — **the last two are recorded nowhere** |
| test / gate defect | 1 | the gate runs `compiler_tests` at one worker under `experiment/env.sh:6`, so the concurrent test passes vacuously there |
| record defect | 12 | nine in R1's two rounds, three of R2's four required corrections |

Every one of the 18 required corrections was closed and re-verified in the tree by the gather stage, which the last climb did not manage — `batched-climb-plan.md` records two of its corrections as simply never made. The three *recommendations* had no such mechanism and two of them were dropped; that is recommendation 1 below.

**On the refusal's class: both answers are true.** The brief had already named the exact defect — "`BaseTask.inATransaction()` was itself repaired in rung 0 (`BaseTask.java:248`, an eagerly built debug string …) and you are on the repaired tree, so do not fix it again" — and the worker read that as *handled* rather than as *evidence that the same defect is at 22 other sites in the same two files*. So a brief clause could have pointed at it. But nothing static proves the absence: the worker's own type probe `probes/P11Obj.fss` writes an object-typed top-level variable and does not crash, and the probe that crashes is that program plus one `atomic` block. One line of program text separated a clean run from a refusal, and only a differential crossing the construct finds it.

## 4. The judge

The judge ran once, on R1's refusal, on the session's model, for 14.6 minutes and 42 tool calls of which only 1.4 minutes were inside a tool — it read and ruled, and built nothing, as `JUDGE.md:2` says of itself.

It read, per its own §"What I read" and confirmed in its transcript: the net diff and the seven `wip/` commits, all three rung documents, and **every specification passage either side cited, at the lines cited** — `atomic.tex` at `sed -n '24,28p'` through `'76,82p'`, `variables.tex` at `115,130p`, `objects.tex` at `198,210p`, `also.tex` at `12,30p`, `components/initialization.tex` at `1,12p` and `15,16p`, `components/source-code.tex` at `330,345p`.

Its ruling cites the specification by line throughout, and the one place the specification is silent it says so and declines to decide: `specRuling` reads "On the default `asString` of an object without one, the prose chapters are silent (`grep -rn asString Specification/basic Specification/basic-lib` finds nothing); nothing was decided under that silence — the crash is removed without choosing a rendering, and the three candidates … are recorded in a ledger row for Pavol." I checked that grep: it returns 0 lines.

It took four decisions of its own and named all four with the alternative each displaced, and its `forPavol` field carries them plus the five unrepaired divergences and the gate's one-worker fact. I can read that field: the workflow's `journal.jsonl` carries every agent's structured result, so this does not rest on `JUDGE.md` alone. What I cannot read is the coordinating session's own turn, so whether the coordinator relayed the field to Pavol verbatim is outside this review; `JUDGE.md:118-123` and `record.md` carry the same content into the tree either way.

## 5. Decisions named, and the four that are not

The two reports and `JUDGE.md` name **22 decisions**, each with the alternative it displaced: ten in `repair-r1-atomic-static/REPORT.md` (five under "The decisions", four under "the four decisions in it", one in the ladder-subset section), seven under `repair-r2-literal-wrap/REPORT.md` §"Decisions taken inside the rung", four in `JUDGE.md` §2 and §7, and one in the commit agent's own result ("I did something slightly different and am naming it as a decision"). The nine `rung*/REPORT.md` of the last climb contain **zero** occurrences of "the alternative was" or of any sentence naming a decision as one.

Against that, the whole of `git diff 49ee5e91..63db7a691 -- ProjectFortress Library` — 542 insertions, 92 deletions, 18 files — yields four choices I cannot find named anywhere, and this is the important list:

input.message:
Committed as **0de59a8a2** on `main` (not pushed; tree clean before and after). Outputs: `explorations/coordinator/repair-batch-review.md` plus `repair-batch-review/parse.py` and `agents.csv`, regenerable with the one command named in the report's head.

**Did the re-architecture work: yes on the four rules the briefs wrote down, no on the one thing they named but did not require.** (1) The specification's prose chapters were opened in **56 of 955 tool calls (5.9%)** against **7 of 1,638 (0.4%)** last climb, and the api listings — the circular authority — **0 times** against 18. (2) The territory map, opened by **none** of the last climb's 36 agents in the four parts the review named, was opened in **15 calls by 8 of 11 agents**. (3) **22 sentences** name a decision as a decision with its alternative, against **0** in the nine earlier reports. Also: 18 of the 20 spec citations in the landed record were opened at the lines cited. What did not take: `Papers/`, `research/` and the spec's `\note{}` passages still had **0 calls**; `design-intent-sources.md` one grep.

**Decisions in the diff not named as decisions** (none changes behaviour): (a) `runtimeSystem/Transaction.java:20` becomes the only file in its package to import a library type (`fortress.AnyType.Any`) — the payload-type decision is named, the dependency direction never mentioned; (b) `MutableStaticBinding.assignHandle` throwing a `CompilerError` (argued at `REPORT.md:76`, no alternative named); (c) `MutableFValue.make` as a static factory (`REPORT.md:80`); (d) three files of the original 2012 corpus edited without the historical-artifact flag `protocol.md:97` asks for at commit time (the rewrite-vs-move choice itself is named well).

**Top three waste items:** `git status`/`log`/`diff`, 114 calls, **22.3 min**; coordinator records re-read, 119 calls, **21.3 min**; poll loops overshooting their sentinel, 35 calls at 5-20 s granularity, **8.2 min**.

**Top three recommendations for `climb-batch-workflow.js`:** (1) add `recommendedRows` to `SKEPTIC_SCHEMA` and a `gatherRole` step closing each — R2's skeptic recommended two ledger rows and neither exists (free); (2) `PREFIX` rule 3: cite the passage, not the grep hit — the batch's only two unopened citations came from `| head -20`, and `basic-integers.tex:569`, one line below, states the answer (free); (3) `GATE_ROLE`: name gate logs `.txt` — `.gitignore:42,46` swallowed all four (free).

Efficiency: 235.4 min for two rungs against ~150 for the old loop, but 2.3× the calls per rung, 68 probe programs, gate down from 25.2% to 5.2% of the clock, concurrency 1.21× at the cap of two. FACTS.md:110's headline figures all reproduce; its 2,600,293 tokens is the sum of each agent's final context, which I measure as 2,600,173.
